lesson.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specAnchors.text: understand how factors may increase the risk of developing coronary heart disease

primer.text: The heart feeds itself first: coronary arteries wrap it, delivering the oxygen and glucose its muscle burns every second. When fatty plaque narrows those arteries, chest pain and heart attacks follow. This note links diet, blood pressure and smoking to the plumbing failure.

modules.title: Coronary Arteries Under Attack
modules.opening: Coronary heart disease begins when fatty plaque, built largely from cholesterol, narrows the arteries supplying the cardiac muscle, restricting flow so the muscle runs short of oxygen.
keyPoints: Coronary arteries supply cardiac muscle with oxygen and glucose.
Plaque deposits build mainly from cholesterol.
Dietary cholesterol arrives from animal products.
The liver also synthesises cholesterol into the blood.
Partial blockage causes angina; complete blockage causes a heart attack.

low.restatement: Fatty layers narrow the heart's own supply lines; partial narrowing aches, total blockage kills muscle.
low.analogy: A kettle's element furring with limescale until it overheats and fails.
low.examPointer: Keep angina (partial) and heart attack (complete) strictly separate in answers.

medium.restatement: Narrowed lumens cut the flow, so the muscle beyond cannot respire aerobically; the blockage's completeness decides pain versus infarction.
medium.analogy: A garden hose kinked slightly versus shut off entirely — trickle versus drought.
medium.examPointer: Name the muscle's need as oxygen for aerobic respiration when explaining the damage.

modules.title: The Risk Factors Behind the Plaques
sourceHeadings: Risk factors of coronary heart disease
modules.opening: Obesity, high blood pressure, high cholesterol and smoking each raise the odds of coronary heart disease — the first by straining the heart, the second by damaging vessel walls, and the last two by feeding and accelerating the plaques.
keyPoints: Obesity strains the heart and can lead to Type 2 diabetes.
High blood pressure damages the artery walls.
High cholesterol speeds plaque build-up toward blockage.
Smoking chemicals raise plaque growth and blood pressure.
Carbon monoxide in smoke cuts the blood's oxygen carriage.

low.restatement: Too much weight, pressure, cholesterol or smoke all push the same disease forward.
low.analogy: Four ways to overload a bridge: heavier trucks, faster traffic, worn cables, missing inspections.
low.examPointer: List all four factors when a question says 'risk factors'; two or three alone lose marks.

medium.restatement: The factors converge on the same endpoint — narrowed coronary lumens — through strain, wall damage, faster deposits and reduced oxygen carriage.
medium.analogy: Four tributaries feeding one flood: different routes, same river.
medium.examPointer: For smoking, name BOTH mechanisms: plaque plus pressure, and carbon monoxide's grip on red cells.

glossary.definition: The vessels wrapping the heart and supplying its muscle.
The fatty deposit, mainly cholesterol, narrowing arterial lumens.
Chest pain caused by partial coronary blockage during exertion.
A smoke gas that binds red cells and cuts oxygen carriage.
